evidence_quotes.quote: This paper reports results of a case study on the relationships between elements of social capital and participation in collective action in the context of addressing water and sanitation issues in the lakeshore village of Usoma, Western Kenya.
The majority of households (86%) used lake water for domestic uses and 42% practiced open defecation.
The survey was administered to every household head in the community between June and August, 2013 with a response rate of 91%.

After interpretation of components based on indicators with high loads on a common factor, we created three additive indices of social capital: informal support networks index, formal support networks index and trust index.
how often in the past year have you joined together with others to address a common issue related to water and sanitation in the community
Model 2 included indices of social capital and exclusion index simultaneously.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household water and sanitation conditions in Usoma, a lakeshore community in Western Kenya, measuring household water sources for cooking and domestic uses (lake water vs. other sources) and sanitation practices (open defecation vs. facility use), though as context and explanatory variables predicting collective action rather than as outcomes.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both readings of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, the paper does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or utility-governance mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules for service access, tariffs/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or regulatory/utility ownership structure); instead, it models cognitive and structural social capital indices (interpersonal trust, group membership, informal/formal support networks), perceived social divisions/peacefulness, socio-demographics (including home ownership only as a predictor of collective action), and baseline water/sanitation use as determinants of individual participation in collective action. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it likewise fails (and would also be excluded because of Criterion 4): psychosocial/community social capital and perceived general support in hypothetical school or animal-disease problems are not legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factors governing service access, and even if informal village water committees or collective action were construed broadly as community governance, no governance factor is evaluated for its effect on water or sanitation access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical data from a cross-sectional household survey administered to household heads in Usoma, Kenya between June and August 2013 using a modified Social Capital Assessment Tool (SOCAT), analyzed via bivariate comparisons, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and binary logistic regression (452 households analyzed in Section 3.1 and Table 1; abstract reports N = 485, 91% response rate).
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: the study's sole analyzed outcome is behavioural participation in collective action in the past year (joining with others to contribute labour/cash or attend village water committee meetings), whereas household water source (lake vs. other sources) and sanitation facility use are entered as independent/explanatory variables predicting collective action. Its 'index of exclusion' is also an explanatory variable measuring perceived community divisions by wealth, landholding, social status, and gender, not exclusion from water or sanitation services.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (household heads in Usoma village, Western Kenya), exposures (social capital indices, perceived community cohesion/division, socio-demographics, and baseline water/sanitation source), outcome (binary participation in water/sanitation collective action), and study design (cross-sectional household survey).

study_design: Cross-sectional household survey analyzed with bivariate statistics, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and binary logistic regression
population_and_sample: Household heads in Usoma, a lakeshore village near Kisumu in Western Kenya; 452 households totaling 2,131 individuals analyzed in text and tables (91% response rate; abstract states N = 485)
exposure: Social capital indices (group membership index, interpersonal trust index, informal support networks index, formal support networks index), perceived community divisions/exclusion and peacefulness, socio-demographic characteristics, and baseline household water source (lake vs. other sources) and sanitation facility use
outcome: Self-reported participation in community collective action related to water and sanitation over the past year (no collective action vs. one to three times, such as contributing labour or cash or attending village water committee meetings)
rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure), and also fails Criterion 4 (Wrong outcome). This cross-sectional household survey in rural Western Kenya investigates how social capital dimensions (trust, group membership, support networks), perceived community cohesion/divisions, socio-demographics, and existing water/sanitation use predict whether household heads participate in community collective action. It neither examines a legal, administrative, regulatory, or rule-type governance mechanism governing service access (Criterion 2 = no under both narrow and plain readings) nor evaluates water or sanitation service access, availability, affordability, or service exclusion as an outcome (Criterion 4 = no; water/sanitation access is entered only as an independent predictor of collective action).
